identification.summary: TIDRONE is the name Trend Micro gave to an unidentified threat actor with links to Chinese-speaking groups, focused on military-related industry chains, particularly drone manufacturers in Taiwan [S1][S3]. Trend Micro's incident-response cases from Taiwan began in early 2024, and its telemetry also showed satellite, financial and other targets in Taiwan, Canada and South Korea [S1][S3]. In May 2025 Trend Micro folded TIDRONE into a broader cluster it calls Earth Ammit, describing TIDRONE as the second of two campaign waves (after VENOM) run between 2023 and 2024 [S2][S4].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro: related activity from early 2024 [S3]; Earth Ammit campaigns span 2023 to 2024 [S2][S4]. CLNTEND was first seen in April 2024 [S3].
identification.notes: Trend Micro names: TIDRONE (2024 report) and Earth Ammit (2025 umbrella cluster covering the VENOM and TIDRONE waves) [S2][S4]. VENOM is the earlier wave aimed at upstream software and service providers [S2][S4]. Trend Micro's Black Hat Asia 2025 talk reportedly linked VENOM to the group Dalbit through shared TTPs and similar tools (per search-result summary; talk not opened) [S4]. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found. Trend Micro's own page dates the TIDRONE report inconsistently across secondary sources (July vs September 2024); this record uses 2024-09 from the URL path and press coverage [S1][S3].

attribution.confidence: Trend Micro assesses the actor as unidentified but linked to Chinese-speaking groups, and the activity as likely espionage [S1][S3]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Per Trend Micro, the actor's operation times and tactics align with other Chinese espionage activity [S3]. Trend Micro describes Earth Ammit as linked to Chinese-speaking APT groups [S2][S4]. Detailed technical attribution evidence in the primary reports was not opened (see gaps).

objectives: Trend Micro assesses espionage against military-related industry chains, especially drone manufacturers, with the Earth Ammit strategy described as compromising trusted vendor networks to reach higher-value downstream targets [S1][S2][S3][S4].

targeting.notes: TIDRONE reporting names Taiwan, Canada and South Korea [S3]; Earth Ammit reporting centres on Taiwan and South Korea [S4][S5]. AhnLab reportedly documented CLNTEND against South Korean companies via ERP software in December 2024 (as reported by The Hacker News and Taiwanese press; AhnLab report not opened) [S4]. Sector list for VENOM comes from secondary summaries of the Trend Micro Earth Ammit report [S4][S5].

capabilities.summary: TIDRONE uses custom backdoors CXCLNT (file upload/download, trace clearing, system information collection, download of further executables) and CLNTEND (a remote access tool first seen April 2024 with broader network protocol support) [S1][S3]. Initial access is unknown, but the same ERP software appeared in several victims, suggesting possible supply-chain distribution; remote access via UltraVNC was observed [S1][S3]. One reported chain has a compromised UltraVNC launching winsrv.exe, then Update.exe, then sideloading a malicious DLL [S3]. Post-exploitation activity included UAC bypass, credential dumping and tools to disable antivirus [S1][S3]. The earlier VENOM wave used mainly open-source tools, web server flaws, web shells and remote access tools [S4][S5].

campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports a first wave aimed at upstream software and service providers using mostly open-source tools, to indirectly reach downstream targets in Taiwan and South Korea.

campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports the CLNTEND remote access tool first observed in April 2024.

campaigns.name: TIDRONE campaign against Taiwan military supply chain
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro incident response in Taiwan found CXCLNT and CLNTEND on drone manufacturers and related military, satellite and financial victims, with a shared ERP software suggesting a supply-chain vector.

campaigns.name: CLNTEND against South Korean companies
campaigns.summary: AhnLab reportedly identified TIDRONE using ERP software to install CLNTEND at South Korean companies (as relayed by secondary coverage).

campaigns.name: Trend Micro Earth Ammit report
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro links VENOM and TIDRONE under the Earth Ammit name and presents the findings at Black Hat Asia 2025.

diamond.adversary: Unidentified actor linked by Trend Micro to Chinese-speaking groups; assessed likely espionage [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Custom backdoors CXCLNT and CLNTEND, DLL sideloading, UltraVNC abuse, credential dumping, UAC bypass, AV-disabling tools [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Not detailed in sources gathered; ERP software and compromised remote-desktop tooling served as delivery paths [S3].
diamond.victim: Taiwanese drone manufacturers and military, satellite and financial organizations; also South Korea and Canada; VENOM wave hit software and service providers [S3][S4][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Targeting of Taiwan's military industrial base is consistent with Trend Micro's espionage assessment and Chinese-speaking actor link; no sponsor stated [S1][S3].
diamond.technology: Shared ERP software and trusted vendor relationships create a supply-chain pivot to downstream defense firms [S2][S3][S4].

gaps: Initial access vector is unknown per Trend Micro; the ERP supply-chain hypothesis is unconfirmed [S3].

The Trend Micro primary reports (TIDRONE 2024, Earth Ammit 2025) could not be fetched; claims rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage. Compilation-time and working-hour evidence for attribution was not verified.
No state sponsor, government attribution, Microsoft name, or MITRE group ID found.
AhnLab's December 2024 report and the Black Hat Asia 2025 Dalbit-VENOM link were not opened directly.
Dating of the TIDRONE report (July vs September 2024) is inconsistent across sources.
Overlap or relationship with other Taiwan-focused Chinese-speaking clusters is not established.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the defense industrial supply chain, notably ERP software, remote-desktop tools and software/service vendors serving drone and satellite firms [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 2: Actors exploit trust in vendors and common enterprise software to reach downstream defense targets [S2][S4]. STEP 3: Observed pattern: vendor or ERP foothold, UltraVNC/DLL sideloading, CXCLNT or CLNTEND backdoor, credential dumping, AV disabling [S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued espionage against Taiwan and South Korea defense suppliers. MDCOA is spread to drone and satellite suppliers in allied nations via shared ERP or managed-service vendors. Candidate indicators: unexpected updates from ERP clients, winsrv.exe/Update.exe launching sideloaded DLLs, UltraVNC installed outside baseline, AV-tamper tooling [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track vendor and ERP software compromise reporting from DIB and allied partners. (2) Authorities: contractor and vendor networks sit outside DoD-owned terrain, so coordinate through DC3 and DIB cybersecurity channels. (3) Mission assurance: inventory ERP and remote-desktop dependencies of drone and satellite programs and segment vendor access [S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Taiwan and South Korea partners given reported targeting [S3][S4].
